final.title: Where a knowledge assistant fits, and where it doesn’t
final.body:
A knowledge assistant is only useful when the answer already lives in your own approved documents. That is the practical line I’d use in a small business: policies, FAQs, product notes, internal process docs, and similar text you already control. If the task needs open-web research, judgment, or human sign-off, it is not really a knowledge-assistant job. It is a people decision with software attached.

That matters when you are comparing manual work, hiring, and a bounded automation investment. Bareni’s self-built knowledge-assistant demo is deliberately narrow: it can ingest MD, PDF, and URL content, run vector search and reranking, generate grounded answers, and show sources. It is a local demo on synthetic data, not a production system, and it should not be mistaken for customer validation or a shortcut around approval.

A simple test helps. Ask: “Could my team answer this by looking in our own documents, or would they need to research outside?” If the honest answer is outside research, the assistant is probably the wrong fit. If the answer is inside your documents, the next step is to audit one recurring workflow against that threshold and see whether it deserves a grounded assistant.
